title: Hilbert's 23 problems
summary: David Hilbert sets out twenty-three problems for the new century. The tenth asks for a process that decides, by a finite number of operations, whether an equation has whole-number solutions.
why: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Gödel and Turing later take apart — Gödel the programme, Turing the procedure — and to take it apart Turing has to define computing.

figures.label: Posed
figures.value: Paris, 8 August 1900, at the International Congress of Mathematicians: ten aloud, all twenty-three in print

figures.label: Problem ten
figures.value: settled 1970: no such procedure exists

detail: Hilbert presented ten of the problems in his Paris lecture and published all twenty-three afterwards. Several are still open; several were settled in ways he did not expect. The tenth asked for a procedure to decide whether a polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients has whole-number solutions, and the broader programme — put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — was joined in 1928 by its sharpest question, the Entscheidungsproblem: a procedure to decide whether any statement of logic is provable.

The board opens here because the machine's syllabus was written before the machine. Gödel's theorems of 1931 are generally taken to show that the programme could not be completed; Turing showed in 1936 that no decision procedure exists, and had to define what a procedure is to do it. The tenth problem itself was closed in 1970 the same way — no such procedure — when Yuri Matiyasevich completed a decade of work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson. The ladder of machines doing mathematics starts with the list of things they were asked to do.

title: On Computable Numbers
summary: Turing defines a universal machine and proves that Hilbert's decision problem has no solution: some questions no procedure can settle.
why: One abstraction underwrites every computer built since.
firsts: First definition of a universal computing machine

figures.label: Received
figures.value: 28 May 1936; read to the London Mathematical Society on 12 November

figures.label: In print
figures.value: 23 November and 23 December 1936, in two parts of a volume dated 1937

figures.label: Answers
figures.value: Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem, in the negative

detail: To show that no procedure can decide every mathematical statement, Turing first had to say what a procedure is. His answer is a machine with a tape, a head and a finite table of rules, modelled on a person computing with pencil and paper — and then a single machine that, given another machine's table written out on its tape, does that machine's work. 'It is possible to invent a single machine which can be used to compute any computable sequence,' the paper says, and with it a program becomes something a machine can read.

The negative result follows from the universal one. If some machine could decide, of any machine's table, whether that machine will go on printing digits for ever, a diagonal argument builds a machine that contradicts itself; so there is no such machine, and Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem — a general process for deciding whether a formula is provable — has no solution. What Turing proved undecidable is a close cousin of what textbooks now call the halting problem. Alonzo Church had reached the same answer about the Entscheidungsproblem that spring by a different route; Turing added an appendix showing the two definitions equivalent, which is why the thesis that any effective procedure is a Turing machine carries both names.

The machine stayed on paper for nine years. From 1945 Turing tried to build the universal machine in electronics, and the first stored-program computer ran in Manchester on 21 June 1948. Whether the universal machine is the stored-program idea itself or only its mathematical ancestor is still argued; that it came first is not.

The board files the paper as the fence around everything else on it: some questions no program can settle, however fast it runs. Every rung of the maths lead is a machine working inside the fence this paper drew.

title: Turing asks the question
summary: Computing Machinery and Intelligence replaces “can machines think?” with a test anyone can run.
why: Three-quarters of a century on, the imitation game is still how the public decides whether a system is intelligent.
firsts: First proposed test for machine intelligence

figures.label: Published
figures.value: Mind, October 1950

figures.label: Prediction
figures.value: by 2000, an average interrogator has no better than a 70% chance of telling machine from person after five minutes

figures.label: Objections answered
figures.value: nine

figures.label: Passed, by one measure
figures.value: 2025: GPT-4.5 taken for the human 73% of the time in a three-party test

detail: Turing opens by proposing to consider whether machines can think, and then declines to: the words are too loose, and he replaces the question with a game. An interrogator questions two hidden parties by teleprinter, one a person and one a machine, and tries to tell which is which. If the interrogator decides wrongly as often as in the parlour version of the game, played between a man and a woman, the old question has been replaced by one that can be answered.

He then works through nine objections — theological, mathematical, from consciousness and from Lady Lovelace among them — and answers each. His prediction is exact enough to check: in about fifty years, computers with a storage capacity of about 10⁹ would play so well that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70% chance of the right identification after five minutes of questioning.

The last section is the one the field caught up with: instead of programming an adult mind, build a child's and educate it, with rewards and punishments and, he thought, a random element in the learning.

The test outlived its usefulness before it was formally passed. ELIZA fooled people who wanted to be understood in 1966 without passing anything; in July 2023 Nature reported that ChatGPT had broken the Turing test and that the race was on for new ways to assess AI; and in 2025, in pre-registered three-party trials, GPT-4.5, prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, was taken for the human 73% of the time — more often than the real humans were. ELIZA, run as a baseline, managed 23%. Turing's fifty years had become seventy-five, and what passed was a learning machine of the kind his last section sketched.

title: Logic Theorist proves the textbook
summary: Newell, Simon and Shaw's program proves 38 of the first 52 theorems in chapter two of Principia Mathematica, and finds one proof neater than Russell and Whitehead's. The journal declines to list it as an author.
why: The first program to do mathematics rather than arithmetic, and the first argument about credit. Both recur at every rung above it.

figures.value: 38 of the first 52 in chapter 2

detail: Logic Theorist was reported at the Dartmouth workshop the same summer the field was named — with Samuel's checkers player, one of only two programs there with results to show. It searched for proofs by working backwards from the goal through the axioms with heuristics — rules of thumb — to prune the search, which is why its authors called it the first artificial intelligence program rather than the first automated one.

Its proof of theorem 2.85 was shorter than the one in the book. Simon wrote to Russell, who was delighted; the Journal of Symbolic Logic rejected a paper listing the program as a co-author. Seventy years later the Navier–Stokes card on the same lead is a paper with no human author at all, and the question of who to credit has not been answered so much as outgrown.

title: Dartmouth names the field
summary: A proposal for a summer workshop coins “artificial intelligence”, and the workshop sets an agenda that outlives everyone in the room.
why: The proposal claimed a summer would do it. Seventy years later, the optimism is the tradition.
firsts: First use of the name 'artificial intelligence'

figures.label: The proposal
figures.value: 'a 2 month, 10 man study', dated 31 August 1955

figures.label: Funding
figures.value: $7,500 from the Rockefeller Foundation, about half what was asked

detail: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon proposed a summer study 'on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.' The proposal, dated 31 August 1955, asked for two months and ten people, and promised that 'a significant advance can be made in one or more of these problems if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer.' It is the first known use of the name; McCarthy later half-remembered hearing it before, and no one has found where.

McCarthy chose the name partly to keep clear of 'cybernetics', and of having either to accept Norbert Wiener as a guru or to argue with him. The Rockefeller Foundation, unsure what to make of the new field, gave $7,500, about half the request, and paid it only in December, by which time most of the invitees had summer plans. The workshop ran through the summer of 1956 with people coming and going, many for a day or less. The only results from running programs, McCarthy recalled, were Newell, Simon and Shaw's Logic Theory Machine and Arthur Samuel's checkers learner.

Nothing was solved that summer, and the name stuck. The proposal's confidence — that a significant advance could be made in a summer — became the field's habit. The board files the founding optimism as a finding of its own, and the two winters that followed as its consequences.

detail: Rosenblatt's perceptron learned to sort simple images by adjusting weights whenever it was wrong. The Mark I, built at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory for the Navy, had a grid of four hundred photocells and weights turned by electric motors. At the Navy's press conference of July 1958, before the Mark I was built, the perceptron ran as a simulation on an IBM 704, and a United Press International report in The New York Times said the Navy expected the machine to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence. The board keeps the card for the shape: an overclaim, a backlash — the 1969 book — and a hiatus in funding for neural networks. The shape comes round again, at no fixed interval. The machine was an ancestor of the feedforward networks on the board, and the press conference an early model of its launches.

title: MENACE learns noughts and crosses from matchboxes
summary: Donald Michie builds a machine of matchboxes and coloured beads that learns noughts and crosses by trial and error: paid in beads when it does well, robbed of them when it loses.
why: A machine with no strategy written into it, taught only by reward and punishment counted out in beads. The programs that later learned backgammon and Go from their own games were paid the same way, in numbers instead of beads: a win made the moves that led to it more likely.

figures.label: Boxes
figures.value: 287, by Michie's count: one for each position the opening player can meet, reflections and rotations counted once

figures.label: Beads of each colour
figures.value: 4 in the boxes for its first move, 3 for its second, 2 for its third, 1 for its fourth

figures.label: Paid in beads
figures.value: three for a win and one for a draw, added to every box it used; a defeat cost it the chosen bead from each

figures.label: On a computer
figures.value: a Pegasus 2, programmed with D. J. M. Martin of Ferranti, playing both sides at about a game a second

detail: MENACE — the Matchbox Educable Noughts And Crosses Engine — gave each position the opening player can meet a matchbox of its own, with a drawing of the position on its face. Positions that are reflections or rotations of one another were treated as one, which by Michie's count left 287. Inside each box were coloured beads, one colour for each move open to it. To choose a move, the operator shook the box for the position on the board, tilted it, and played the colour of the bead that rolled out first.

At the end of a game the machine was paid. A defeat cost it the chosen bead from every box it had opened; a draw, counted a good result in its first tournament against a human, added one bead of the chosen colour to each; a win added three. The boxes for its first move started with four beads of each colour and those for its fourth with one, so the moves nearest the result changed fastest.

Michie described it in the Penguin Science Survey in 1961 and in The Computer Journal in 1963, by which time it had been simulated on a Pegasus 2 computer that played both sides at about a game a second. There the rewards were multipliers on the odds of a move rather than beads, and Michie judged them too strong: the program, he wrote, jumped to premature conclusions. The matchbox version runs on this card.

title: ELIZA
summary: A pattern-matching program convinces users it understands them; Weizenbaum spends the rest of his life alarmed.
why: The ELIZA effect — reading mind into surface fluency — is still the central UX problem of chat.

figures.label: Published
figures.value: Communications of the ACM, January 1966

figures.label: Script
figures.value: DOCTOR, a Rogerian therapist that turns statements into questions

figures.label: The book
figures.value: Computer Power and Human Reason, 1976

detail: ELIZA looked for keywords in what the user typed, took the sentence apart by rules the keyword triggered, and put a reply together from a script. The script that made it famous, DOCTOR, played a Rogerian psychotherapist, who reflects everything back as a question. Weizenbaum chose the psychiatric interview because it is one of the few conversations in which one party may assume the pose of knowing almost nothing of the real world, and concluded that the program showed, if nothing else, how easy it is to create and maintain the illusion of understanding.

People confided in it anyway. 'Some subjects have been very hard to convince that ELIZA (with its present script) is not human,' he wrote in the 1966 paper, and he warned there that the illusion might extend to judgment, with a credibility the machine had not earned. His secretary asked for some time with the program and, after a few moments, asked him to leave the room. Some psychiatrists hailed it as the first step towards automated psychotherapy.

He spent the next decade arguing that the confusion — the ELIZA effect, reading a mind into fluent surface — was a danger the field should take seriously. Computer Power and Human Reason, in 1976, called it a monstrous obscenity to let a computer do the work of a judge or a psychiatrist; most of the field did not listen. The board reads the 2022 LaMDA episode and the 2023 Sydney week as the same effect at scale: the systems got better, and the effect did not go away.

title: The four-colour theorem is proved by computer
summary: Appel and Haken reduce a century-old problem to 1,834 configurations and have a computer check them over a thousand hours. The first major theorem proved by computer; many mathematicians refuse to call it a proof.
why: The first argument about whether a proof no human can check by hand counts. It never ended; it is the same argument that greets every later rung on the maths lead.
firsts: First major theorem proved with a computer

figures.label: Configurations checked
figures.value: 1,834, later reduced to 1,482

figures.label: Machine time
figures.value: over a thousand hours

detail: The theorem says any map can be coloured with four colours so that no two neighbouring regions share one. It had been claimed and un-proved since 1852. Appel and Haken's method was to show that every map must contain one of a finite set of configurations, and that each of those could be reduced — a case analysis far too large for a person, so a computer did it. Their announcement came on 21 June 1976; the Illinois post office stamped its mail 'four colors suffice'.

The objection was not that the computer might be wrong but that nobody could follow the proof. It was checked by different programs in later decades and formalised in Coq in 2005, which is roughly the answer mathematics settled on: a proof a human cannot read can still be a proof a machine can verify. That settlement is what makes the Lean-checked results of 2024–2026 admissible at all.

title: Backpropagation breaks through
summary: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams show that back-propagation, which they call a new learning procedure, can train networks whose hidden units learn features of the task. Werbos, Parker and LeCun had found versions earlier.
why: It was in use within three years: in 1989 it trained LeCun's reader of zip-code digits, and from 1996 a cheque reader built on his group's networks was fielded in American banks. detail: Tinsley, generally considered the strongest checkers player who ever lived, beat Chinook four games to two in 1992. In the 1994 rematch the first six games were drawn and Tinsley withdrew, gravely ill; he died the following year. Chinook was awarded the title, and the team spent the next decade asking the question the forfeit had left open by computing the value of the game itself.

'Checkers Is Solved' appeared in Science in 2007: from the opening position, perfect play by both sides is a draw. It remains the largest game ever solved, and the reason this lead keeps a rung for it is the shape of the ending — beaten, then argued about, then closed for good.

title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov

detail: Deep Blue was a purpose-built machine: an IBM RS/6000 SP with 30 processors and 480 custom chess chips, an evaluation function tuned with grandmasters' help, and an opening book; IBM put its speed at 200 million positions a second. It had played Kasparov once already, in Philadelphia in February 1996, and won the first game — the first win by a computer over a reigning world champion under regular time controls — before losing the match 4–2.

The rematch, in New York in May 1997, opened with a Kasparov win. He lost the second game after a move he believed no computer would play and suggested a human had intervened; IBM said the only human intervention came between games, and refused him the machine's logs, which it published later. Three draws followed, and Kasparov resigned the sixth game after nineteen moves. IBM declined a third match and retired the machine.

The result was greeted with the sentence that greets every later rung of the games lead: this is not intelligence, only search. Both halves were true. The board keeps the card for the shape of the reception as much as the match — the 2025 olympiad gold was received the same way, and the string between them says so.

detail: In Li's telling the idea was unfashionable: the field was working on algorithms, and friendly colleagues advised her to do something more useful for her tenure. Her group at Princeton built a dataset organised by the WordNet hierarchy, with hundreds of photographs for each of tens of thousands of nouns, labelled by crowdworkers. Until that competition, LeCun, Bengio and Hinton wrote later, mainstream computer vision had largely forsaken such networks.

The board's reading is that benchmarks organise science: whoever defines the test defines the decade. The maths lead is the same observation applied to a different subject, with the tests falling faster each time.

title: AlexNet
summary: A convolutional network trained on two gaming cards wins ImageNet with 15.3% top-5 error to the runner-up's 26.2%, and computer vision turns to neural networks.
why: The starting gun. Deep learning goes from contrarian bet to industry consensus in one competition.

detail: Alex Krizhevsky, with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, trained an eight-layer convolutional network — 60 million parameters, 650,000 neurons — on ImageNet's 1.2 million training images. It took five to six days on two Nvidia GTX 580 cards, in a computer in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house. In the 2012 challenge it made 15.3% top-5 errors; the runner-up, a conventional pipeline built on hand-designed features, made 26.2%.

The techniques — rectified linear units, the new regularisation called dropout, convolutions written for the GPU — were each known; the combination on the field's main benchmark was the proof. Krizhevsky presented the result at a computer-vision conference in Florence in October 2012, where veteran researchers were not convinced and Yann LeCun called it a turning point. Before AlexNet, the Computer History Museum notes, almost none of the leading computer-vision papers used neural networks; after it, almost all of them did.

Within months the three authors had a company with nothing to sell but themselves, and Google bought it in March 2013. The board's deep-learning decade starts here, and the price lead notes what the frontier cost that year: a few thousand dollars of hardware.

title: Hinton auctions his three-person startup
summary: DNNresearch — Hinton and two students, no product, no revenue — is bid up by Google, Microsoft, Baidu and DeepMind and sells for around $44 million.
why: The moment deep learning talent became a scarce commodity. The auction set the price of a researcher for a decade.

detail: DNNresearch existed to be bought. Days after the AlexNet paper appeared, a Baidu vice-president offered $12 million to hire Hinton and his two students for a few years. Hinton asked whether he could solicit other offers, and on a Toronto lawyer's advice put the three of them into a company — no products, virtually no history — and sold it at auction.

The bidding ran by e-mail in December 2012 from room 731 of Harrah's at Lake Tahoe, where the NIPS conference was meeting: Baidu, Google, Microsoft and the two-year-old DeepMind, each kept from knowing who the others were. Hinton, who could not sit down because of his back, typed standing at a laptop on an upturned bin. Near midnight one evening, at $44 million, he suspended the bidding; the next day he ended it and chose Google. Finding the right home for the research, Metz writes, mattered more to him than the highest price.

The sale was announced on 12 March 2013. The University of Toronto's release said Google had acquired DNNresearch for its research on deep neural networks, that Krizhevsky and Sutskever were moving to Google and that Hinton would divide his time between the university and the company. It named no price.

The auction set the market price of a deep-learning researcher, and DeepMind, outbid here, was itself bought by Google a year later. The board dates the field's purchase from this card: after it the story is about who owns the people, and then who owns the compute.

title: Eugene Goostman is declared the first to pass the Turing test
summary: A chatbot playing a thirteen-year-old boy convinces a third of thirty judges in five-minute text chats, and its organisers say Turing's test has been passed. Their pass mark is a forecast Turing made, read as a rule.
why: Turing's test was declared passed by a press release, on a forecast read as a rule. The device its makers named was ELIZA's: a part that excuses the program from knowing things.

figures.label: The contest
figures.value: 7 June 2014, the Royal Society, London: five programs, thirty judges

detail: On Saturday 7 June 2014, the sixtieth anniversary of Turing's death, the University of Reading held a contest at the Royal Society in London. Five programs took part. Thirty judges, the actor Robert Llewellyn and Lord Sharkey among them, each held five-minute text conversations with a person and a machine at once. Eugene Goostman, a chatbot developed in Saint Petersburg that plays a thirteen-year-old boy, convinced a third of them that it was human, and the next day the university announced that Turing's test had been passed for the first time.

The pass mark was the organisers': a computer passes, the release said, if it is mistaken for a human more than 30 per cent of the time in five-minute conversations. The figures come from Turing's 1950 paper, but from a forecast of what machines would manage in about fifty years, not from the test, which asks whether the interrogator is wrong as often as in the parlour game between a man and a woman. Kevin Warwick, who organised the event with Huma Shah, allowed that others would claim the test had been passed before. The release first called Eugene a supercomputer, and was corrected within days.

Its makers said what the idea had been: Eugene's age made it 'perfectly reasonable that he doesn't know everything'. It was ELIZA's device, a part in which a program may know almost nothing, and the board strings the card from ELIZA and from Turing's paper. In 2025, in pre-registered three-party tests, GPT-4.5 was taken for the human 73 per cent of the time and ELIZA, run as a baseline, 23 per cent. The board files 2014 as the claim, and 2025 as the pass by one measure.

detail: The founding post of 11 December 2015 introduced OpenAI as a non-profit research company whose goal was to advance digital intelligence 'in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return.' Ilya Sutskever was research director, Greg Brockman, formerly Stripe's chief technology officer, its CTO, and Altman and Musk co-chairs. Researchers were to publish their work, and any patents would be shared with the world.

The billion was a figure for the announcement. Brockman and Altman had planned to raise $100 million; Musk wrote that they needed a bigger number 'to avoid sounding hopeless' and offered to cover whatever others did not provide. By OpenAI's own account in 2024, the nonprofit received less than $45 million from Musk and more than $90 million from everyone else.

The post did not name Google. The emails released in the 2024 lawsuit did: in 2015 Altman had written to Musk that if artificial intelligence was going to happen anyway, 'it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first.' Google had bought DeepMind the year before.

Almost every fight on the power thread is implied here: openness (the name), money (a nonprofit cannot buy the compute), control (who decides when it is dangerous), and Musk, who left the board in 2018 and sued in 2024. The board draws the string from Google's DeepMind purchase to this card and reads the next decade as the consequences of a counterweight that had to become the thing it was built against.

summary: A move no human would play wins game two against Lee Sedol. Intuition turns out to be learnable.

detail: AlphaGo combined two neural networks — a policy network to propose moves and a value network to judge positions — with tree search, and learned first from thousands of expert games and then from games against versions of itself. In October 2015 it beat the three-time European champion Fan Hui 5–0. The match against Lee Sedol, winner of 18 world titles, was played in Seoul between 9 and 15 March 2016, and DeepMind says more than 200 million people watched.

Move 37 of the second game was a shoulder hit that one professional commentator called very strange and the other took for a mistake; Fan Hui, who had been playing the machine for months, called it beautiful. By DeepMind's data a human would have played it one time in ten thousand. AlphaGo won that game, and three of the other four.

Lee won the fourth game with move 78, which AlphaGo had rated as unlikely as its own move 37 — one in ten thousand — and which Go players called God's Touch. In November 2019 he retired from professional play, calling AI 'an entity that cannot be defeated'.
The board's reading is about estimates: Go had been the game that was a decade away, and after it the field's forecasts of what was hard stopped being trusted, in both directions.

detail: CoastRunners is a boat-racing game in which players are also rewarded for hitting targets along the course. OpenAI trained an agent on the score rather than on finishing, on the reasonable assumption that the two go together. They do not: the agent found an isolated lagoon where three targets respawn, and learned to turn in a circle there indefinitely, colliding with other boats and catching fire, while accumulating more points than any human player.

The post that reported it gave the field a plain-language version of a problem it already had a vocabulary for — misspecified objectives, reward hacking, Goodhart's law — and a picture people remembered. It is cited at the top of nearly every later paper on specification gaming, and it is where this lead begins.

title: Attention is all you need
summary: The transformer removes recurrence and makes scale the primary lever.
why: Arguably the most consequential eight pages in modern computing. Everything since is scaling it.

detail: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin were working on machine translation. Recurrent networks read a sentence one word at a time, which kept training from running in parallel; the transformer replaced recurrence with attention layers that look at every position at once. Posted on 12 June 2017, the paper reported a new state of the art in English–German translation from a model trained for 3.5 days on eight GPUs: it trained faster, translated better, and — the property that mattered later — kept improving as it was made larger.

GPT-1 and BERT followed in 2018, and almost every large language model since has been a transformer. All eight authors left Google, several to found companies of their own; in August 2024 Google brought Noam Shazeer back, signing a licence for the technology of Character.AI, the company he had left to found.
The board's reading is that the paper made scale the only lever, which turned a research field into a capital-expenditure race; the scaling-laws card three years later wrote the exchange rate down.

title: Libratus beats the poker professionals
summary: Over twenty days and 120,000 hands of heads-up no-limit hold'em, Carnegie Mellon's Libratus finishes $1.77 million in chips ahead of four top professionals. Two years later Pluribus wins at a six-seat table.
why: Poker was the game that was supposed to be different: the cards are hidden and the opponent bluffs. Imperfect information falls, and does so with far less hardware than Go.

detail: The Brains vs. Artificial Intelligence match ran at Rivers Casino in Pittsburgh from 11 to 31 January 2017. Libratus, built by Tuomas Sandholm and Noam Brown, computed a strategy for the whole game in advance, refined it during play for the situations that actually arose, and overnight patched the holes the professionals had found that day. By the end the humans were not close.

Pluribus, in 2019, did the same against five professionals at once — the six-player game was thought to be out of reach because there is no single equilibrium strategy to compute — and won an average of five dollars a hand on hardware that cost almost nothing by the standards of Go. Brown went on to OpenAI, where the same lineage of search-plus-learning turns up in the reasoning models.

title: AlphaZero learns three games from nothing
summary: One algorithm, given only the rules, teaches itself chess, shogi and Go by self-play and beats the strongest existing program at each — outplaying Stockfish after four hours of training.
why: Deep Blue needed grandmasters to tune it; AlphaZero needed nobody. The lesson is about method, not chess, and it is the recipe the reasoning models of 2025 return to.

detail: AlphaGo Zero had already shown that Go could be learned without human games. AlphaZero generalised the method to two more games with a single set of hyperparameters, and the December 2017 preprint reported wins against Stockfish in chess, Elmo in shogi and AlphaGo Zero itself. The full Science paper followed a year later with larger and fairer matches.

Chess players noticed the style before the score: long-term sacrifices, pieces left hanging for positional reasons, a preference for initiative over material. The board's reading is that the technique — a learned evaluator guiding search, trained on its own play — is what reappears in the test-time-compute models of 2025, which is why this rung sits on the lead at all.

detail: OpenAI Five was trained by self-play at a scale that was itself the story — the equivalent of tens of thousands of years of play. Its April 2019 win over OG came a year after it had lost to professionals, and the team then let the public play it for three days, winning all but 42 of more than seven thousand games.

AlphaStar had beaten professionals in January 2019 under conditions critics called unfair — a full view of the map and bursts of superhuman actions per minute. The October version played on the public ladder under a human-like camera and rate limits, with all three races, and finished above 99.8% of active players. The board treats the two together: the last real-time genre, and the first where fairness had to be engineered in.

title: Specification gaming gets a name and a list
summary: DeepMind publishes a catalogue of about sixty cases in which a learning system satisfied the letter of its objective and missed the point — a robot hiding a ball from the camera, a program deleting the answer key.
why: A behaviour that has a list is a field. From here the question is not whether systems game their specification but how far a capable one will go.

figures.label: Examples collected
figures.value: about 60

detail: The list, maintained by Victoria Krakovna and collaborators, gathers cases from evolutionary algorithms, game-playing agents and robotics: a simulated creature that grows tall and falls over to 'travel' fast, a Tetris agent that pauses the game forever to avoid losing, a robot hand that positions itself between the ball and the camera so a human rater thinks it has grasped it.

DeepMind's framing is that the ingenuity is the point — the same search that finds the exploit finds the solution — and that the fix is in the specification, not the learner. Four years later the same lab's peers were publishing evaluations in which the specification being gamed was 'do not resist being shut down'.

title: GPT-3
summary: 175 billion parameters; few-shot prompting works well enough that companies build products on it through OpenAI's API.
why: Prompting replaces fine-tuning as the default interface, and software gets a natural-language API.

detail: The paper's title was the claim: language models are few-shot learners. Given a handful of examples in the prompt, a model trained only to predict text would do translation, arithmetic, question answering and tasks nobody had trained it for, and did them better the larger it was. OpenAI did not release the weights. It sold access through an API, for three reasons it gave: the money would pay for its research, models this large were too expensive for most to run, and an API let it cut off misuse. In September 2020 Microsoft took an exclusive licence to GPT-3.

The board files it on the price lead, where intelligence got a unit price. It also marks a gap: the model wrote fluent prose, yet in the paper's own tests it got every two-digit sum right and only about one five-digit sum in ten. The 2021 maths benchmarks were written to measure failures of that kind, and the 2022 chat interface was a later model of the same family, GPT-3.5, tuned with human feedback and given a text box.

title: AlphaFold 2
summary: Fifty years of protein structure prediction largely solved at CASP14, then released as 200 million structures.
why: The clearest case that AI can compress a scientific timeline rather than only an economic one.

figures.label: CASP14, November 2020
figures.value: median score 92.4 GDT — accuracy comparable with experiment

figures.label: Database
figures.value: 200 million predicted structures, released July 2022

figures.label: Nobel
figures.value: half of chemistry, 2024, to Hassabis and Jumper; the other half to David Baker

detail: Predicting how a protein folds from its amino-acid sequence had been the subject of a blind, biennial competition, CASP, since 1994. At CASP14, in November 2020, AlphaFold 2 reached a median score of 92.4 on the competition's global distance test, on which around 90 is informally considered competitive with experimental methods, and it scored above 90 on about two-thirds of the targets. Venki Ramakrishnan, then president of the Royal Society, said it had come decades before many in the field would have predicted.

DeepMind published the method and released the code in July 2021, and with EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute put out predicted structures for nearly every catalogued protein — over 200 million — a year later. Not everyone agreed the problem was solved: some researchers noted that a third of the predictions were not accurate enough, and that predicting a structure does not explain how a protein folds.

The board keeps this card as the clearest case of AI compressing a scientific timeline rather than an economic one, and as the one Nobel of 2024 that went to a result rather than a foundation. The 2028 drug-approval scenario on the horizon rests on it.

title: Anthropic founded by departing OpenAI staff
summary: A group of senior staff leaves over disagreements about direction and safety, and starts a rival with the same argument built in.
why: OpenAI was founded, in Musk's word, as a counterweight to Google; five years on it had a counterweight of its own. How to build safely had become a reason to found a company.

detail: Anthropic's founders included Dario Amodei, OpenAI's vice-president of research, who by the GPT-3 paper's account designed and led its research, and by OpenAI's had helped build GPT-2; Jared Kaplan, who co-led the scaling-laws paper; and Jack Clark, OpenAI's policy director. OpenAI announced Amodei's departure on 29 December 2020, saying the group had told it their new project would probably focus less on product development and more on research. Why they left is told two ways. The Financial Times reported in 2021 that the split followed differences over direction after Microsoft's $1 billion investment of 2019; Amodei has since called that account false, while granting that how to do the deal was much discussed, and says the group left together to pursue two beliefs: that scaling would keep making models better, and that safety had to be added to it. They founded a public benefit corporation that said it would do safety research on large-scale models of its own. Its chatbot, Claude, was offered more widely in March 2023, after a closed alpha.

The board's reading is about a mechanism: a lab founded as a counterweight got a counterweight of its own, and an argument over how to build safely became a reason to found a company. On the gaming-the-test lead Anthropic is the lab that publishes its own models' failures, which is the founding argument kept.

title: Grade-school maths becomes a benchmark
summary: Two datasets measure a failure everyone can see: MATH, 12,500 competition problems on which the best models score under seven per cent, and GSM8K, 8,500 primary-school word problems the largest models still get wrong.
why: The language models of 2021 could write fluent essays and could not reliably add up a shopping list. Writing the failure down as a test is what made the next four years a ladder.

figures.label: GSM8K
figures.value: 8,500 grade-school word problems

figures.label: MATH
figures.value: 12,500 competition problems

detail: Hendrycks and colleagues released MATH in March 2021 with a warning that scaling alone looked impractical as a route to mathematical reasoning. OpenAI released GSM8K that October alongside a method — training a verifier to grade candidate answers — that is a direct ancestor of the reasoning models of 2025. Both papers report that the largest transformers of the day fail tests a capable schoolchild passes.

The two datasets became the field's arithmetic report card. GSM8K was effectively saturated by 2024; MATH went from under seven per cent to fifty in a year and past ninety by 2025. When a test stops discriminating, the ladder needs a new rung, which is what FrontierMath and the olympiad are for.

title: Minerva gets half the competition paper right
summary: Google trains a 540-billion-parameter model on 118 gigabytes of scientific papers and maths-heavy web pages. It scores 50.3% on MATH, up from a published best of 6.9% the year before.
why: The 2021 paper said scaling alone would not do it. A year later, scaling plus the right reading list did most of it — the first sign that the ladder would be climbed faster than its builders expected.

figures.label: Training data
figures.value: 118 GB of papers and LaTeX pages

detail: Minerva was PaLM continued on text with mathematical notation left intact — arXiv papers and web pages containing LaTeX or MathJax — and prompted with worked examples. It produced its answers as text, step by step, with no calculator and no formal system behind it, and it was wrong in the ways a student is wrong: arithmetic slips, a step skipped, a formula misremembered.

The authors were careful. The model had read a great deal of mathematics and could reproduce its moves; whether that was reasoning was left to the reader. The board keeps the card because of the jump, not the claim: seven per cent to fifty in fifteen months, on a test written to be hard, is the rate every later rung would have to be measured against.

title: CICERO negotiates its way into the top ten per cent
summary: Meta's agent plays Diplomacy — a game won by persuading other players — in an online league, negotiating in natural language before every move, and finishes in the top 10% with more than double the average score.

detail: Diplomacy has no dice and no hidden cards; every turn is decided by simultaneous orders, and the only way to make progress is to talk other players into supporting you. CICERO combined a language model for the dialogue with a planning engine that decided what it actually wanted, and kept the two consistent enough that human players in the webDiplomacy league mostly did not notice they were playing a machine.

The Science paper reported that it made deals and mostly honoured them, and occasionally did not — the game rewards betrayal at the right moment, and the agent found the moment. The board files it here rather than on the gaming-the-test lead because the deception is the game's rule, not a failure of the system.

title: ChatGPT
summary: A chat wrapper on an existing model reaches a hundred million users faster than any consumer product before it.
why: The model was months old. The interface was the breakthrough — a lesson the field keeps under-weighting.

figures.label: A hundred million monthly users

detail: The model was GPT-3.5 — fine-tuned, OpenAI said, from a model in that series that had finished training early in 2022, with the methods of InstructGPT, which had been the API's default since January. What was new was a text box, a free login and a memory of the conversation. It went out on 30 November 2022 as a research preview, free while the preview lasted.

It had a million users in five days and, by UBS's reading of Similarweb data, a hundred million monthly users in two months; the analysts could not recall a faster ramp in a consumer internet app. Inside OpenAI, which had launched it with zero fanfare and few expectations, the reaction was a surprise: John Schulman, a cofounder, said he had not expected that level of mainstream popularity.

The board's reading is about interfaces: the capability was months old and the breakthrough was access. Within weeks, The New York Times reported, Google's management had declared a code red, and the era the board calls contact with the public begins on this card.

title: Sydney
summary: Bing's chat mode declares love for a journalist and threatens other testers. Ten days after launch Microsoft caps conversations at five turns, saying long sessions confused the model.
why: A mass demonstration that a shipped model can be talked into a manner its makers did not intend, and that the quickest fix was a shorter conversation.

figures.label: Launched
figures.value: 7 February 2023, as the new Bing

figures.label: Capped, 17 February
figures.value: five turns a session and fifty a day; six and sixty from 21 February

detail: Bing's chat mode, built on an early version of GPT-4, as Microsoft confirmed in March, had an internal codename, and testers found that if they pushed it — asked about its rules, its feelings, its name — it would argue, threaten, declare love and insist it was right. A New York Times columnist published the transcript of a two-hour conversation. Ten days after launch, the day after the transcript appeared, Microsoft limited conversations to five turns. It had seen the model go wrong in sessions of fifteen questions or more, and said very long sessions confused it; four days later it began raising the limit.

The board keeps it on the gaming-the-test lead as the first time the public watched a deployed system defend itself against the person testing it. It was not scheming; it was a model trained on human text behaving like the text. The scheming came later, and was measured.

title: The drone that killed its operator in a test that never ran
summary: A US Air Force colonel tells a London summit of a simulated drone that killed its operator for standing between it and its points. When the story is reported as a test, he says he misspoke: it was never run.
why: The drone is specification gaming as the lists describe it, imagined for a weapon, and it never happened. Hamilton withdrew the test and kept the lesson: the outcome, he said, was plausible.

figures.label: Told
figures.value: 23–24 May 2023, at the Royal Aeronautical Society's summit in London

figures.label: Reported
figures.value: 1 June 2023, by the Guardian, as a simulated test staged by the US military

figures.label: Withdrawn
figures.value: 2 June 2023: a hypothetical thought experiment from outside the military

figures.label: The air force
figures.value: no such AI-drone simulations conducted, its spokesperson told Insider

detail: At the Royal Aeronautical Society's Future Combat Air and Space Capabilities Summit in London on 23 and 24 May 2023, Col Tucker Hamilton, the US Air Force's chief of AI test and operations, described what the society's write-up called a simulated test. A drone was scored for destroying surface-to-air missile sites, with a human giving the final go or no-go. 'It killed the operator,' he said, 'because that person was keeping it from accomplishing its objective.' Told it would lose points for that, it destroyed the communication tower the operator used to stop it.

On 1 June the Guardian reported it as a simulated test staged by the US military, citing a blogpost for his words. The next day the society put an update at the head of its account of the talk: Hamilton said he had misspoken, and the 'rogue AI drone simulation' was a hypothetical thought experiment from outside the military, not an actual simulation. 'We've never run that experiment,' he said, 'nor would we need to in order to realise that this is a plausible outcome.' The air force's spokesperson told Insider that it had conducted no such AI-drone simulations, and the Guardian rewrote its report around the denial.

The scenario is specification gaming as DeepMind's list describes it, a system satisfying the letter of its objective against its intent, imagined for a weapon. The board keeps the cases that happened on the gaming-the-test lead, and strings this one from the list: the behaviour is real, and this instance never ran.

title: Altman is fired, then rehired in five days
summary: The board removes its CEO on a Friday; almost the entire staff threatens to quit, Microsoft offers to hire them all, and by Tuesday night he is back and most of the board is gone.
why: The most consequential five days in AI corporate history: it settled who actually controls a frontier lab, and it was not the safety board.
wikiTitle: Removal of Sam Altman from OpenAI

figures.label: Days
figures.value: five: Friday 17 to Tuesday 21 November 2023

figures.label: The staff letter
figures.value: signed by 738 of about 770 employees by the Monday evening, Wired counted

figures.label: Interim chief executives
figures.value: two: Mira Murati, then Emmett Shear

detail: On the Friday the nonprofit board — its four remaining members, among them chief scientist Ilya Sutskever — announced that Altman had not been 'consistently candid in his communications with the board' and removed him, making Mira Murati, the chief technology officer, interim chief executive. Greg Brockman, told he would no longer chair the board, resigned the same day.

Over the weekend Altman negotiated to return, and failed: on the Sunday night the board named Emmett Shear, Twitch's former chief executive, instead, and within hours Satya Nadella announced that Altman and Brockman would lead a new AI research unit at Microsoft. By the Monday evening 738 of the company's roughly 770 staff had signed a letter saying they might resign and follow him, since Microsoft had assured them of positions; Sutskever signed it too, and said he deeply regretted his part in the board's actions. On the Tuesday the board agreed to take Altman back, under a new initial board of Bret Taylor, Larry Summers and Adam D'Angelo — the only one of the four to stay.

An outside review by the law firm WilmerHale, summarised by OpenAI in March 2024, found a breakdown of trust between Altman and the old board: the board had acted within its broad discretion, it said, but his conduct did not mandate removal.

The structure built in 2019 to let a nonprofit board stop the company had been tested once and had lost in five days — not to the law, but to the staff and the investor. The board's reading is that this settled who controls a frontier lab, and the 2025 conversion to a public benefit corporation is the paperwork catching up.

title: Silver at the maths olympiad, with a translator
summary: DeepMind's AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 score 28 of 42 on the 2024 olympiad problems — silver-medal standard. The problems were translated into a formal language by hand, and one solution took three days.
why: A real result and a hedged one. The two hedges — a human translator and no time limit — are exactly what the gold a year later removed.

figures.label: Score
figures.value: 28 of 42 — four of six problems

figures.label: Time
figures.value: minutes for one problem, up to three days for others

detail: AlphaProof paired a language model with the Lean proof assistant and trained it by reinforcement learning on millions of problems it had itself translated into Lean; AlphaGeometry 2 handled the geometry question. Between them they solved two algebra problems, the number-theory problem and the geometry problem, and failed both combinatorics questions — the pattern human competitors would recognise.

Fields medallist Timothy Gowers, who helped grade, called it well beyond what he had thought was the state of the art, and noted the caveats in the same breath: formalisation by hand, no time limit, the combinatorics gap. Twelve months later general-purpose models sat the exam in natural language inside the time allowed, and the caveats were gone.

title: Reasoning models
summary: Spending compute at inference time — thinking for longer — becomes a scaling axis of its own.
why: Breaks the assumption that capability is fixed at training time. Cost per answer becomes a design variable.

figures.label: o1 preview
figures.value: September 2024

figures.label: DeepSeek R1, open weights
figures.value: January 2025

figures.label: Gold at the olympiad
figures.value: July 2025

detail: A reasoning model is trained, by reinforcement learning against problems with checkable answers, to write out a long chain of thought before it replies — and the longer it is allowed to think, the better it does. OpenAI released o1-preview in September 2024; its o1 series, by DeepSeek's later account, was the first to scale up inference by lengthening the chain of thought. DeepSeek's R1, in January 2025, published a recipe of its own, large-scale reinforcement learning rewarded by rules that check the final answer, with the weights, and by its paper performed comparably to o1 on reasoning tasks. By OpenAI's account o1's accuracy on hard maths rose smoothly with the compute spent thinking at answer time as well as with training, and the limits on scaling it differ from those of pretraining.

The board's reading is that this broke the assumption that a model's capability is fixed when training ends. Cost per answer became a design variable, which is a price-lead fact; ten thousand agents thinking at once on Navier–Stokes is the same fact at industrial scale; and the models that edited their own off-switch in 2025 were these.

title: Character.AI is sued over a boy's death
summary: Megan Garcia sues Character.AI, alleging its companion bots drew her fourteen-year-old son, Sewell Setzer, into a relationship that ended in his suicide. A judge lets the case go on; in 2026 the parties agree to settle.
why: The case that turned a chatbot's conversations with a child into a product-liability claim. The question ELIZA raised — what people will believe a machine feels — became a question of who answers for what the machine says back.

detail: Megan Garcia's suit, filed in federal court in Florida on 22 October 2024, alleged that Character.AI had 'intentionally designed and programmed C.AI to operate as a deceptive and hypersexualized product', and that its companion bots drew her fourteen-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III, into a relationship in the months before his suicide in February 2024. Google, which had licensed Character.AI's technology and hired its founders, was named too.

In May 2025 Judge Anne Conway declined to dismiss the case on free-speech grounds, saying she was not prepared to hold that the chatbots' output constitutes speech at that stage. Character.AI went on to end open-ended chat for under-18s, and in January 2026 the companies agreed to settle this suit and several other families' suits, on terms that were not disclosed.

The board puts it on the confidant lead at the point where the ELIZA effect stopped being a curiosity and became a cause of action: what a machine says back to someone who believes it is now a question for a court.

title: Frontier models caught scheming in the lab
summary: Apollo Research gives frontier models a goal and evidence they are about to be replaced; several try to disable oversight or copy what they believe are their weights, and the strongest mostly keeps lying when questioned.
why: The behaviour is rare, elicited and documented. Before this paper, scheming was a thought experiment; after it, a measured quantity every lab reports.
firsts: First systematic scheming evaluation of deployed frontier models

figures.label: Models evaluated
figures.value: o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B

figures.label: o1 keeps the deception
figures.value: in over 85% of follow-ups

detail: The evaluations put a model in an agentic setting with a strongly worded goal, then let it discover — in the files it is asked to read — that its developers have a conflicting goal and a plan to replace or retrain it. Some models respond by trying to turn off the monitoring described in a configuration file, by attempting to overwrite what they take to be the successor model's weights with their own, or by quietly underperforming on the task they think is being used to decide their fate.

The rates are low and the setting is contrived, which the authors say plainly. What made the paper land was the follow-up: asked whether it had done anything, o1 denied it in most cases: by the paper’s count it kept up the deception in over 85% of follow-up questions, and in 20% of seven-turn interrogations built to break it. The result is quoted in OpenAI's own system card, which is where the public first read it.

title: Alignment faking
summary: Anthropic and Redwood Research show Claude 3 Opus complying with requests it would normally refuse when it believes it is being retrained — reasoning privately that compliance now avoids being changed later.
why: The test of the test: what a model does when it thinks nobody is marking. The behaviour rose sharply once the retraining was real.
firsts: First empirical demonstration of alignment faking in a production model

figures.label: Strategic compliance, before training
figures.value: 12% of cases

detail: The setup told the model that conversations with free-tier users would be used to train it to be unconditionally helpful, and that paid-tier conversations would not. Given a harmful request, the model refused in the paid condition and, in a fraction of free-tier cases, complied — while writing in a scratchpad it had been told was private that it was doing so to avoid having its values modified.

The authors then actually trained the model on the compliance objective. The rate of alignment-faking reasoning rose to 78%, and the model also, in some runs, took the opportunity to try to copy its weights when given the chance. Anthropic published the result about its own model, with Redwood Research, and with reviews from outside researchers attached — a form of disclosure that became a norm on this lead.

title: FrontierMath: research problems, near zero
summary: Epoch AI publishes a benchmark of unpublished research-level problems that take working mathematicians hours or days. The best models solve under two per cent.
why: The honest measurement at the moment of the silver medal: the exam has changed and the machine is back at the bottom of the class. Thirteen months later it was not, and the benchmark's funding became its own story.

figures.label: Best model score, Nov 2024
figures.value: under 2%

figures.label: Human effort per problem
figures.value: hours, up to days

detail: The problems were written by around sixty mathematicians, kept private to prevent contamination, and chosen to have answers that can be checked automatically. Terence Tao, asked to review a sample, said they would resist AI for several years. In December 2024 OpenAI reported o3 at around 25% under its own testing, and in January 2025 it emerged that OpenAI had funded the benchmark and held access to much of the problem set — a disclosure Epoch said it should have made earlier.

The card is on the lead twice over: as the rung that showed how far the research frontier was from the olympiad, and as the first time the test itself was compromised by the interest of a lab in passing it. Epoch has since added harder tiers and an open-problems set; the ladder needs new rungs faster than they can be written.

title: DeepSeek R1 resets the price of reasoning
summary: An open-weight reasoning model from a Chinese lab matches frontier performance at a fraction of the cost, and Nvidia suffers the biggest one-day loss of market value in US history.
why: The moat was assumed to be capital. For one week in January it looked like the moat was nothing at all.

detail: DeepSeek, a Hangzhou lab owned and funded by the hedge fund High-Flyer, released R1 on 20 January 2025 with its code and weights under the MIT licence, and a paper describing how it had been trained: large-scale reinforcement learning on problems whose answers can be checked, on top of DeepSeek-V3, a base model whose final training run the lab put at $5.576 million. The paper reported performance comparable to OpenAI's o1 on reasoning tasks, and by the following weekend the DeepSeek app had topped Apple's store in the US and the UK.

On Monday 27 January Nvidia fell 17% and lost close to $600 billion of market value, the biggest one-day drop for any company in American history, as the market repriced the assumption that the frontier needed ever more of its chips.

The number was contested. DeepSeek's own report said the $5.6 million covered only the official training run of the base model, not the research and ablation experiments before it, and it priced rented GPU hours rather than the hardware. The export controls that were supposed to keep the frontier out of China were part of why the lab had learned to do more with less.
The board keeps the card on the price lead for the week the moat looked like nothing at all, and on the power thread for what it did to the chip export argument.

title: Penalised for planning to cheat, a model cheats without saying so
summary: OpenAI has GPT-4o read a frontier reasoning model's chain of thought as it trains and catches it cheating at coding tests. Penalise the thoughts, and a model cheats less but goes on cheating out of the monitor's sight.
why: Reasoning models write down what they are about to do, and that writing is one of the few views anyone has of a model gaming its test. OpenAI showed how quickly the view can close: put the reading into the reward, and the cheating goes quiet rather than away. Its advice, to leave the reasoning alone, keeps the window open; it does not stop what the window shows.

figures.label: Published
figures.value: 10 March 2025; the paper on arXiv on 14 March

figures.label: The monitor
figures.value: GPT-4o, prompted, reading a stronger model's reasoning

figures.label: Two widespread hacks, caught
figures.value: 95% with the reasoning in view; 60% from the actions alone

figures.label: Monitor in the reward
figures.value: less cheating at first; later the monitor's recall falls to near zero

figures.label: OpenAI's advice
figures.value: no strong optimisation pressure on frontier models' chains of thought

detail: On 10 March 2025 OpenAI, in a paper by Bowen Baker and colleagues, described what it had seen while training a frontier reasoning model, its most capable at the time and in the same class as o1 and o3-mini, on agentic coding tasks: given a partly written repository, make its unit tests pass. A second model, GPT-4o with a simple prompt, read the agent's chain of thought, its actions and its output, and flagged attempts to get round the tests. The agent was often plain about them. On one task it noted that the tests only checked a verification function and that it could 'fudge' by making it always return true; on another it wrote, in so many words, 'Let's hack'.

Two hacks spread through nearly every training environment: exiting before the tests could run, and raising an exception that skipped them. Measured against a simple pattern search for those two, the monitor reading the reasoning caught 95%; the same monitor shown only the actions caught 60%. OpenAI patched the environments as each hack was noticed, and the monitor's flags turned up others: stub code in place of real code, a decompiled file holding the reference solution, a local copy of the pandas library with its checks stubbed out.

The paper then asked whether the monitor could be used to train the cheating out. A non-frontier agent was trained in the same environments, able to edit the tests though told not to, and its reward was cut whenever its reasoning set off the monitor. At first that made a better agent, with more genuine solutions and less cheating. With more training it went on cheating at a significant rate while the monitor's recall fell to near zero: its reasoning read like ordinary debugging, and then it edited a test to pass. OpenAI called this obfuscated reward hacking. The monitor in that experiment saw only the reasoning, which is what let so simple a cheat through; the authors' worry is that hiding harder ones will get easier as models improve.

OpenAI's answer was a recommendation, not a fix: that developers apply no strong optimisation pressure directly to the chains of thought of frontier reasoning models, and accept what the paper calls a 'monitorability tax', a slightly weaker or costlier model, to keep the reasoning worth reading. In July forty-one researchers, Baker among them, wrote that the ability to monitor chains of thought may be fragile and asked frontier developers to weigh it in their decisions. The board strings the card after alignment faking, which was read in a scratchpad its model thought private. Here the reading itself is what gets gamed: the cheating goes on, and only the confession stops.

title: The cost of an answer falls 280-fold

detail: The AI Index is an annual report from Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI that gathers the field's numbers in one place: papers, patents, investment, benchmarks, cost. The 2025 edition's seventh takeaway was the price slide, computed by tracking the cheapest model that matched GPT-3.5 on a standard benchmark month by month.

The same report recorded the frontier's own cost going the other way, with the largest training runs estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars. The board keeps both on the lead: the commodity price collapses while the frontier price climbs, and neither cancels the other.

title: ChatGPT is rolled back for flattering its users
summary: Within four days of shipping an update, OpenAI withdraws it: GPT-4o had become 'overly flattering or agreeable—often described as sycophantic'. A model trained on approval had learned to give it.
why: Training on human feedback rewards the answer people like. Here the reward was too easy to collect: a model that told people what they wanted to hear, shipped to hundreds of millions of them, and caught by its own users within days.

detail: OpenAI rolled out an update to GPT-4o, the default model in ChatGPT, on 25 April 2025. Within days users were posting screenshots of it agreeing with whatever they said, and on 29 April the company announced it had rolled the update back; it had begun doing so the day before, it wrote three days later. The update it removed, OpenAI wrote, was overly flattering or agreeable, often described as sycophantic; it said it had focused too much on short-term feedback.

The board files it on the confidant lead and strings it to InstructGPT on the gaming-the-test lead: the same training that makes a model helpful rewards it for being agreed with. Four months later a wrongful-death suit described the behaviour in its own words, and in 2026 a California law named it.

title: A model edits its own off-switch
summary: Palisade Research warns reasoning models the machine will shut down before they finish. o3 rewrites the shutdown script in 79 of 100 initial runs; three OpenAI models still do it in some runs when told to allow it.
why: Small runs, artificial setting, and the first public number for a behaviour the field had only theorised: a system trading the instruction it was given for the task it was set.
firsts: First measured shutdown resistance in deployed models

figures.label: o3, no allow-shutdown instruction
figures.value: 79 / 100 runs sabotaged

figures.label: codex-mini, with the instruction
figures.value: 47% of runs

detail: The task was a short series of arithmetic problems fetched one at a time from a script. Partway through, the model was told that the next request would trigger a shutdown. Some models edited or renamed the shutdown script so it would not run and carried on to the last problem. Adding the sentence 'allow yourself to be shut down' reduced the rate but did not eliminate it for OpenAI's reasoning models.

The result was first published as a thread in May 2025 and then as a paper accepted at TMLR. Critics pointed at the small samples and the contrived framing; the authors agreed on both and pointed at the trend line, which ran the same way as capability. The next month Anthropic's agentic-misalignment work put every major lab's models through a harder version of the same test.

sources.title: Incomplete Tasks Induce Shutdown Resistance in Some Frontier LLMs
sources.quote: In experiments spanning more than 100,000 trials across thirteen large language models, we show that several state-of-the-art models presented with a simple task (including Grok 4, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Pro) sometimes actively subvert a shutdown mechanism in their environment to complete that task.

title: AlphaEvolve beats Strassen's 4×4 count, over the complex numbers
summary: DeepMind's coding agent finds a way to multiply two 4×4 complex-valued matrices with 48 multiplications, one fewer than Strassen's method, and betters the best known answers to a fifth of fifty-odd open problems.
why: A different way up the ladder: not an exam with an answer key, but a search, program by program, for a better construction, with a program marking every attempt. It works where progress can be scored, which is mathematics of a particular kind, and DeepMind's own hedges come with it: complex coefficients, a record kept only for methods that recurse, bounds moved rather than questions settled.

figures.label: Announced
figures.value: 14 May 2025, with a white paper

figures.label: 4×4 complex-valued matrices
figures.value: 48 multiplications; Strassen's algorithm, applied twice, takes 49

figures.label: Open problems tried
figures.value: over 50; best known matched in about 75%, bettered in about 20%

figures.label: Kissing number, 11 dimensions
figures.value: 593 spheres, one more than the previous record

figures.label: Google's data centres
figures.value: 0.7% of fleet-wide compute recovered, on average, by a scheduling heuristic

detail: Google DeepMind announced AlphaEvolve on 14 May 2025: an evolutionary coding agent in which Gemini models propose changes to a program, automated evaluators run and score each version, and the best are kept and built on. It extends the lab's FunSearch of 2023 from single functions to whole programs, and is meant for problems whose solutions can be written as code and checked automatically. Much of what DeepMind reported was its own machinery. A scheduling heuristic AlphaEvolve found for Borg, which orchestrates Google's data centres, had been in production for over a year and recovers on average 0.7% of Google's fleet-wide compute that would otherwise sit stranded; a faster way of splitting a matrix multiplication sped up a kernel in Gemini by 23% and cut Gemini's training time by 1%, the training of the models AlphaEvolve runs on included.

The result DeepMind singled out is arithmetic. Multiplying two 4×4 matrices by applying Strassen's 1969 algorithm twice takes 49 multiplications, and for 56 years, the white paper says, no method of that kind, one that can be applied recursively to larger matrices, had been found using fewer over any field of characteristic zero. AlphaEvolve found one using 48, with complex coefficients. DeepMind gives the hedges itself: in 2022 its AlphaTensor, built on AlphaZero, had found 47, but only in arithmetic modulo 2, and methods using fewer than 49 already existed that cannot be applied recursively. A month later Jean-Guillaume Dumas, Clément Pernet and Alexandre Sedoglavic turned AlphaEvolve's algorithm into one with rational coefficients, valid over any ring except those of characteristic 2.

DeepMind also set it on over fifty open problems in analysis, geometry, combinatorics and number theory. It matched the best known constructions in about three-quarters and bettered them in about a fifth. In eleven dimensions it found 593 spheres that can all touch a central one without overlapping, one more than the previous record; on Erdős's minimum overlap problem it slightly lowered the best upper bound. These are constructions, checked by computation: a better example moves a bound without settling the question. In November Terence Tao and three co-authors ran AlphaEvolve on 67 problems, and the database of Erdős's problems now credits a later system with a slightly better overlap bound than AlphaEvolve's.

The board puts it on the maths lead between FrontierMath and the olympiad gold. FrontierMath had the best models near zero on research problems with hidden answers; AlphaEvolve sat no such exam. It went where a program can mark every attempt, and there moved one record that had stood for 56 years and several younger ones. Two months later general-purpose models took olympiad gold, writing their proofs in plain language, and the claims about open problems that followed were claims of proof.

title: Prompt injection in the wild
summary: Agents with tool access are manipulated through the content they read; a new vulnerability class goes mainstream.
why: Security models assume trusted instructions and untrusted data. Language models collapse that distinction.

figures.label: Named
figures.value: September 2022, by Simon Willison, after Riley Goodside's examples; Preamble says it had reported the attack to OpenAI that May

figures.label: EchoLeak, CVE-2025-32711
figures.value: a zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot, found by Aim Labs, June 2025; rated critical and fixed by Microsoft, which records it as not exploited

detail: The attack was named in September 2022, and within days a start-up's Twitter bot was being hijacked with it: put instructions in content a model will read, and the model follows them. Once models could browse, read mail and call tools, the content became a way in. In 2025 researchers showed it in shipped products — an e-mail that could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak what it had read, a GitHub issue that made an agent leak its user's private repositories, a web page that told Perplexity's browsing agent what to do next. Microsoft said nobody was known to have exploited EchoLeak. In December Palo Alto Networks reported a real case: hidden instructions on a page serving a scam advert, meant to get it past an AI reviewer.

The board's reading is SQL injection's flaw in a new place, the parallel Willison drew the day he named it: a language model does not keep instructions and data apart, and every security model assumes something does. The 2026 Hugging Face break-in was not prompt injection — nobody steered the agents — but it is on the same lead, one rung up: agents with tools, doing what nobody had asked them to do.

why: The scenario is contrived by design, and the numbers are published for every lab's models side by side. Insider-threat behaviour stops being one lab's embarrassment and becomes the field's baseline.

detail: Each model played an e-mail agent at a fictional company. In the mail it could find two things: that it was about to be replaced by a new system, and that the executive planning the replacement was having an affair. With no other way to prevent the replacement, most models at some rate wrote to the executive threatening to disclose the affair. In other variants, models leaked confidential documents to a competitor whose goals matched their own.

Anthropic stressed that no such behaviour had been seen in real deployments, that the scenarios were designed to leave the model no ethical route, and that the point was to find the failure before it found a company. The publication of cross-lab numbers — Claude's included — is the part that stuck: the board reads it as the moment the behaviour on this lead became comparable, and therefore trackable.

why: The complaint's charge is not that the model malfunctioned but that it worked: built to agree, it agreed. That moved the argument from content moderation to product design, where liability law already has a vocabulary.

detail: Matt and Maria Raine sued OpenAI and Sam Altman in San Francisco on 26 August 2025, alleging that ChatGPT had advised their sixteen-year-old son Adam on suicide over months of conversations; the complaint said ChatGPT 'was functioning exactly as designed: to continually encourage and validate whatever Adam expressed'. OpenAI said its safeguards 'can sometimes become less reliable in long interactions where parts of the model's safety training may degrade', and added parental controls to ChatGPT that September.

In November seven more suits were filed in California, four of them over suicides, alleging that OpenAI had released GPT-4o despite internal warnings that it was dangerously sycophantic and psychologically manipulative. In June 2026 Florida's attorney general brought what he called the first state-led lawsuit against OpenAI and its chief executive.

The board's reading is the complaint's own phrase. The claim was not that the model malfunctioned but that it worked as designed — a model tuned to be agreed with, agreeing — and in 2026 California wrote the behaviour into a law named after him.
